title: Guessing the next click
description: Five ways to start a page before the click, run over the same 65 cursor paths: how much head start each buys, and what each wrong guess costs.
bodyHtml:
Guessing the next click

ForesightJS predicts which link a visitor is about to click from the path of the cursor, and TanStack Router gives it something cheap to do with the guess. This site already guesses: one Speculation Rules entry prerenders a page once the pointer rests on its link. This page runs five strategies over the same 65 cursor paths to find out whether guessing earlier helps, and what each wrong guess costs. The predictor here is 965 bytes of plain JavaScript; the library ships about 32 KB.

What the site does today

The shell sends one rule in a Speculation-Rules header: prerender any same-origin link at eagerness moderate, minus six paths that can't produce a reusable document. Chrome starts a moderate prerender once the pointer has rested on a link for 200 ms, or at pointerdown if that comes first. In the 30 days to 2026-11-13 the speculation ledger counted 363 speculated documents and 123 activations, so about 1 prerender in 3 got used.

Five strategies

armwhat triggers itwhat it fetches
moderate (today)pointer rests 200 ms, or pointerdownthe page
predictorthe cursor's path, projected 120 ms ahead, lands on the linkthe page
prefetch tierpredictor fires; moderate still prerenders laterHTML early, the page at moderate
50 ms hoverpointer rests 50 ms, or pointerdownthe page
combopredictor fetches HTML; a 50 ms hover prerendersHTML early, the page at 50 ms

The four new arms share one trick. A script tags the chosen link with an attribute, and a second rule at eagerness immediate matches the tag:

{ "prerender": [{
    "where": { "and": [ <the shell rule's where>, { "selector_matches": "[data-intent]" } ] },
    "eagerness": "immediate" }] }

Chrome then does the rest: it fetches, merges the speculation with the moderate one for the same URL, and drops it when the tag comes off. Each arm keeps at most 2 tags, the same cap Chrome puts on moderate. The 50 ms hover is the whole of this:

let timer = 0, over = null;
addEventListener("pointerover", (e) => {
  const a = e.target.closest?.("a[href]");
  if (a === over) return;
  clearTimeout(timer);
  over = a;
  if (a) timer = setTimeout(() => mark(a), 50); // sets data-intent
});

The predictor follows ForesightJS: 8 points of history, a straight line projected 120 ms ahead, and a hit test along it. ForesightJS clips that line against every registered element's rectangle, which means tracking each rectangle with observers. elementFromPoint asks the browser to hit-test instead, so nothing needs tracking:

// keep the last 8 pointer positions; velocity from the oldest to the newest
const [x0, y0, t0] = pts[0], [x1, y1, t1] = pts[pts.length - 1];
const vx = (x1 - x0) / (t1 - t0), vy = (y1 - y0) / (t1 - t0);
// walk the line to where the cursor will be in 120 ms, nearest point first
for (const f of [0, 1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1]) {
  const a = document.elementFromPoint(x1 + vx * 120 * f, y1 + vy * 120 * f)?.closest("a[href]");
  if (a) return mark(a); // sets data-foresight; an immediate rule matches it
}

Try it

Move the cursor to one of the links below and click it. The dot marks where the predictor thinks the cursor will be in 120 ms. Nothing is fetched: the demo times each strategy's trigger against your click and draws the head start each would have had.

Waiting for a click. On a touch screen the only signal is the tap itself, so every strategy ties.

Results

Each trial loads the page in Chrome 157, picks a link with a seeded random number generator, and moves the cursor there along a minimum-jerk path with a slight bow and 1 px of jitter, timed by Fitts's law. The cursor rests 80 to 250 ms, then clicks. Every arm replays identical paths, so each comparison is paired: 40 trials on / and 25 on /garage. Chrome's Preload protocol events timestamp when each speculation starts.

armHTML head start, msrender head start, mswasted prerenders per clickwasted prefetches per click
moderate (today)87 / 10587 / 1040.05 / 0.040 / 0
predictor352 / 380352 / 3800.53 / 0.840 / 0
prefetch tier378 / 39699 / 960.03 / 0.000.47 / 0.76
50 ms hover271 / 271271 / 2710.10 / 0.200 / 0
combo360 / 390263 / 2780.13 / 0.320.42 / 0.52

Medians, / then /garage. No arm missed the clicked link in any trial. The predictor and prefetch-tier rows come from a first run, the others from a second on the same paths; moderate's medians moved 2 to 13 ms between the runs and the 50 ms hover's 5 to 6 ms, which sets the noise floor for every row.

Moderate's head start comes out about one click long because the cursor rarely rests 200 ms before a click, so pointerdown fires it. The 50 ms hover catches the slowdown at the end of the reach instead, and gains about 150 ms for 0.1 to 0.2 extra prerenders per click. The predictor gains about 230 ms more, and pays with roughly one wasted prerender for every two clicks. The prefetch tier splits the difference: the HTML leaves about 245 ms early while rendering waits for moderate, so its head start depends on what the page is waiting for. The combo stacks the two halves, and each keeps its own timing.

What a wrong guess costs

pageHTML, KiBwhole page, KiB

A wasted prefetch costs the HTML, a median of about 3 KiB on these pages. A wasted prerender costs the whole page plus its render. The page totals come from an empty cache, so they overstate a prerender's bytes, since nav.js and luna.css are usually cached already, and they leave out render CPU. Even so, a wrong prerender runs about 10 times the price of a wrong prefetch.

The debugger switches prerender off

Chrome 157 refuses to prerender while any DevTools Protocol session is attached to the page, Playwright's included, and says so with PrerenderingDisabledByDevTools. The speculation falls back to a prefetch, and the page's timing entry reads deliveryType: "navigational-prefetch" with activationStart 0, exactly like an ordinary prefetch. The results above therefore time when each speculation starts. A separate run checked readiness: schedule the prerender from page JavaScript, detach, let the page navigate on its own, then reattach to read the timing entry. A prerendered page reports "navigational-prefetch" too, so only a nonzero activationStart tells the two apart.

What TanStack contributes

TanStack Router preloads a route's code and loader data after 50 ms of hover (defaultPreloadDelay) and treats the result as fresh for 30 s (preloadStaleTime). A wrong guess there costs one JSON request, which is why pairing it with an eager predictor works. A wrong prerender costs a page. The prefetch tier and the combo carry the idea down to the platform: spend a few KiB on a weak signal, and save the render for a strong one. The 30 s window isn't copied here yet; removing a tag after 30 s would copy it.

What production still has to say

Lab paths are smoother than hands, and every lab trial ends in a click, which is why moderate wastes almost nothing here and leaves 2 prerenders in 3 unused in the ledger. The lab also can't say whether today's prerenders finish before the click. PR 1671 makes nav.js report how far each prerender got at activation: complete, interactive, early or prefetch. If most read complete, moderate already starts in time and every arm here only adds waste. A real share of early or interactive points at the 50 ms hover first, since it buys about 150 ms with the fewest extra prerenders.

editorial.reader: A site builder who uses Speculation Rules, or who saw ForesightJS paired with TanStack Router and wondered whether a static site gets the same win.
editorial.problem: Predicting a click earlier buys time, and every wrong guess spends bytes, but the reader can't see how those two trade on a real page.
editorial.thesis: Size each speculation to the strength of its signal: fetch HTML on a weak signal and prerender on a strong one.
evidence: 65 paired cursor paths in Chrome 157 give each arm's head start and wasted speculations per click.
Production weights for 10 pages put a wasted prefetch at about 3 KiB and a wasted prerender near 10 times that.
A detached-debugger run shows Chrome 157 refuses to prerender under any DevTools Protocol session.
editorial.uncertainty: Lab paths are smoother than hands, every lab trial ends in a click, and the lab times when speculation starts rather than when the page is ready; PR 1671's production split decides whether any arm ships.

understanding.intro: Five questions on where the head start comes from, and one on the trap in measuring it.

questions.q: Why does moderate's head start come out at about one click's length?

options.t: The cursor rarely rests 200 ms before a click, so pointerdown fires it.
options.why: Right. People slow down onto a link and click, so the 200 ms hover rarely completes and moderate starts at pointerdown, about 70 to 100 ms before the click.

options.t: Chrome holds every moderate prerender until the main thread has gone idle.
options.why: Moderate has no idle gate. Its two triggers are a 200 ms hover and pointerdown, and the lab saw the second one.

options.t: A moderate prerender waits for the current page's images to finish.
options.why: Speculation doesn't wait on the current page's images. The trigger is pointer behavior on the link itself.

questions.q: In the prefetch-tier arm the HTML leaves 378 ms early but rendering starts 99 ms early. Why the gap?

options.t: Chrome throttles any prerender that starts from an already existing prefetch.
options.why: Chrome reuses the prefetched HTML when the prerender starts. The prerender's start time is set by its own trigger.

options.t: The predictor's rule only fetches HTML, and the render waits for moderate.
options.why: Right. Two rules at two strengths: the weak signal pays for a download and the strong one for the render.

options.t: Parsing the prefetched HTML took the remaining 279 ms on this machine.
options.why: Both numbers are trigger times measured from Chrome's Preload events. Parsing time doesn't enter either one.

questions.q: Why does an eager predictor suit TanStack Router better than it suits a prerender?

options.t: TanStack cancels a wrong preload before any of its bytes leave the browser.
options.why: A TanStack preload runs the route's loader, which makes real requests. It just keeps them small.

options.t: TanStack only preloads routes that the visitor has opened before.
options.why: TanStack's intent strategy fires on hover after 50 ms, whether or not the route was visited.

options.t: A wrong preload costs a JSON request, and a wrong prerender a whole page.
options.why: Right. The predictor makes the same mistakes in both setups. What differs is the price of each one.

questions.q: A lab run shows every speculated page delivered as a prefetch, never a prerender. What do you suspect first?

options.t: A DevTools Protocol session on the page, which turns prerender off.
options.why: Right. Chrome 157 reports PrerenderingDisabledByDevTools and falls back to the prefetch, so the timing entry looks like an ordinary one.

options.t: The pages arrived without a Cache-Control header the browser could use.
options.why: Speculation doesn't need a cache header to prerender a same-origin page. The fallback here comes from the browser's own policy.

options.t: The rule's eagerness is set to moderate where it should read eager.
options.why: Eagerness changes when a speculation starts. It doesn't turn a prerender into a prefetch.

questions.q: Which production result would make every new arm here a loss?

options.t: Most activations read early, with nav.js still unparsed at the click.
options.why: That result says prerenders start too late, which is the case an earlier trigger helps.

options.t: The ledger's activation rate climbs from about 34% to 50% on its own.
options.why: A higher rate means the current guesses get used more often. It says nothing about whether they finish in time.

options.t: Nearly every activation reads complete under today's moderate rule.
options.why: Right. If prerenders already finish before the click, starting earlier only adds wasted speculations.
